title: Tactical PR splitting & undo guide
content:
Purpose:
A compact, practical reference for when and how to split large changes into safer PRs and fast rollback patterns. Notes to self — half checklist, half war-room playbook.

Context and assumptions:
- Target audience: me + oncall devs + reviewers who need an escape hatch for risky PRs.
- We prefer: small surface-area PRs, backwards-compatible defaults, feature flags, and quick reverts.
- This is deliberately opinionated — tradeoffs ranked: safety > speed > elegance.

When to split a PR (red flags):
- Touches > 3 subsystems (api, runtime, infra, console) in one commit.
- Database migration + behavioral change in same PR.
- > 200 lines of net change without isolated unit tests.
- Introduces new runtime dependency or native binary change.
- Requires infra changes + client changes to deploy in lockstep.

Chunking strategies (practical patterns):
1) By contract first:
   - PR A: schema/contract additions (feature-flagged, default-off), tests for new contract.
   - PR B: implementation that consumes schema (can be merged later).
2) By read/write separation (for DB changes):
   - PR 1: write-side safely write-backwards, keep old reads.
   - PR 2: backfill/migrate.
   - PR 3: flip reads.
3) By dependency layering:
   - infra / ops / schema PRs first (minimal changes, no logic).
   - library/runtime change PRs next.
   - product-facing PRs last.
4) Quick UX/Docs follow-up: avoid mixing copy/UX polish with behavior changes.

Minimal PR checklist (pre-merge):
- Does CI run unit + integration tests relevant to changed modules? If not, add targeted tests.
- Is there a feature flag for behavior toggles that could be turned off at runtime?
- Has the change been tested locally against a small dataset (~100 rows) for DB changes?
- Are schema migrations backward compatible or write-once?
- Does commit history contain a clear revert point (one logical commit for the change)?
- PR description includes rollout plan & rollback steps.
- Link to monitoring/alerting runbooks if this impacts latency or memory.

Rollback strategies (fast paths):
A) Soft toggle (recommended):
   - Put behavior behind a flag that can be toggled in console.
   - Rollback = flip flag + quick smoke test.
B) Revert commit + hotfix PR:
   - If immediate revert needed and feature flag not present, open a revert PR that reverts the single commit(s). Use the GitHub revert button when possible.
   - Follow with a trimmed hotfix PR to address the root cause.
C) Fallback route (routing-level):
   - If change reduced capacity/latency, add a routing rule to send traffic to older region/pool.

Fast revert commands cheatsheet (local):
- Find the offending merge commit: git log --merges --oneline --since=\"2 weeks\"
- Revert by hash: git revert -m 1 <merge-commit-hash>  # preserves history
- If large, create a targeted revert branch: git checkout -b revert/pr-1234 && git revert -m 1 <hash> && gh pr create --fill

Revert PR checklist (what to include in revert PR):
- Describe immediate symptoms and data points (error rates, latency spikes).
- Timestamps of first bad deploy and signal.
- CI results + smoke test runbook.
- Short-term mitigation steps (flags toggled, routes changed).
- Plan for root-cause fix and whether revert should be rolled forward or stay.

CI/observability gating suggestions (quick wins):
- Add a small regression test that asserts no absence of expected telemetry (e.g., request count for endpoint).
- Add an e2e probe to run post-merge that triggers critical path with mocked downstreams.
- For perf-sensitive changes, add a smoke perf job (100 synthetic requests).

Review checklist for reviewers (fast scan):
- Surface area: can you describe the change in 2 sentences? If not, ask for split.
- Safety nets: migrations, flags, feature switches present?
- Tests: do unit tests assert behavior; do integration tests exist for cross-service changes?
- Logging/metrics: did author add metrics to help detect regressions?
- Backwards compatibility: are old clients still supported?
- Rollout plan: does the author suggest canary %s and duration?

Follow-ups & follow-through (post-merge):
- Add a tiny synthetic monitor tied to the release (alert threshold x2 baseline).
- Schedule 24–48h post-merge check-in on slack #oncall and add to incident board if regression spotted.
- Convert temporary feature flag -> permanent config or remove if not needed after 90 days.
- If revert happened, add a retro note with timeline and root cause.

Examples (short scenarios):
- Scenario: runtime hotfix + schema change in same PR.
  Action: split into: schema (default-off), runtime hotfix (no schema), then implementation.
- Scenario: cross-repo change touching console + serving runtime.
  Action: console PR with feature flag + small UI, runtime PR behind flag; coordinate deployment order.

Notes to self / heuristics:
- If a change touches infra/config + logic, assume it needs at least 3 PRs.
- Prefer many small explicit commits over one big squash for easier reverts.
- Always include the migration preview command for DB changes in PR description.
- When in doubt, add a flag. Rewriting history to remove a risky commit is ok only before merge. After merge, prefer explicit revert PRs for audit.

Open TODOs (things to formalize later):
- Template: automatic "rollback steps" snippet in our PR template.
- Small script for generating a revert PR given merge hash (wrap gh + git revert).
- Add a CI job to reject PRs that combine migrations + behavioral changes without explicit flag.

Quick links (for war-room use):
- How to toggle feature flags: /console/flags (ops link)
- Revert PR example: https://github.com/redwood-inference/repo/pull/1122

End notes:
Keeping this short so I can paste into a PR description or Slack thread during an incident. Save as checklist for next few releases.

-- Ivy
